werk/led-zeppelin-houses-of-the-holy.text:
In 1972 Led Zeppelin travelled with the Rolling Stones' mobile studio to Stargroves, Mick Jagger's country house in Hampshire. The guitarist Jimmy Page and the bassist John Paul Jones had set up a studio at home, so they arrived with complete compositions and arrangements. Further recording followed at Olympic Studios and Electric Lady Studios. Page produced, and Eddie Kramer was the engineer and mixed the album.

The heavy, dark blues rock sound of their earlier records gave way to a clearer, more spacious rock sound, with a sharper guitar tone. It is the group's most varied record: swing in Dancing Days, reggae in D'yer Mak'er and psychedelia in No Quarter. The Rain Song came about after George Harrison complained that the group never made ballads. The title track was left on the shelf and only appeared on a later record. The critical response was mixed, but the album became a great commercial success.
werk/led-zeppelin-houses-of-the-holy.listen: Listen in The Rain Song to the Mellotron strings that Jones added and to the shifting dynamics of the song.

werk/led-zeppelin-physical-graffiti.text:
A first attempt to record new songs foundered in November 1973 at Headley Grange, the country house in Hampshire where the band had worked before. In January and February 1974 Led Zeppelin returned and recorded eight tracks there. The informal atmosphere left room to improvise and refine arrangements. Because the new tracks almost filled three sides of an LP, it became a double album, supplemented with seven tracks left over from earlier records.

The record covers hard rock, progressive rock, funk, blues and folk. Kashmir sounds Eastern-tinged and orchestral, Trampled Under Foot is a driving funk rocker and Bron-Yr-Aur is an instrumental piece for acoustic guitar. The release was delayed because the sleeve with die-cut windows was difficult to produce. In the United Kingdom the album went straight to number one.
werk/led-zeppelin-physical-graffiti.listen: Listen to Trampled Under Foot and notice how the rhythm keeps driving forward, with a funk feel that you would not immediately expect from a hard rock band.

werk/ledisi-lost-en-found.text:
After her second album, Feeling Orange but Sometimes Blue, from 2002, Ledisi's career stalled. She ran into money worries and went through a divorce, and considered leaving music for Broadway. In 2006 she opened a show for Chaka Khan in Washington. Ron Goldstein, the head of Verve Records, was in the audience and offered her a contract afterwards. Lost & Found, her third album, was released on 28 August 2007. She worked on the album with, among others, Rex Rideout, Lorenzo Johnson and Luther Mano Hanes.

It sounds like traditional rhythm and blues with influences from funk, hip hop and soul, and is about love, strength and relaxation. She wrote Alright because she herself doubted whether she wanted to stay in music. The album received good reviews, reached the top ten of the American R&B chart and earned nominations for a Grammy for Best R&B Album and for Best New Artist.
werk/ledisi-lost-en-found.listen: Listen to Alright and notice how personal the vocals sound. The song is about her own life and her doubts about whether to carry on.

werk/ledisi-pieces-of-me.text:
After a break in her career, Ledisi wanted to make a record that leaned on traditional rhythm and blues and stood out against contemporary pop. From late 2010 she recorded the album in studios in California, with Rex Rideout, Chuck Harmony and Claude Kelly and with writers she had not worked with before. The result sounds milder, with influences from funk, hip hop and soul. She called it her most personal album.

John Legend co-wrote I Miss You Now and Jaheim sings on Stay Together. The album was released in 2011, was received mostly well and was the first of her studio albums to reach the top ten of the Billboard 200. It was nominated for a Grammy for Best R&B Album.
werk/ledisi-pieces-of-me.listen: Listen to Stay Together and notice how the voices of Ledisi and Jaheim alternate and come together.

werk/ledisi-the-truth.text:
After Pieces of Me, Ledisi took a break to act; she appeared in Leave It on the Floor and Selma, in which she played Mahalia Jackson. In 2013 she returned to music and recorded the album in a few months, faster than ever. She again worked with Rex Rideout, Chuck Harmony and Claude Kelly.

The lyrics come from her own experience of a long relationship that did not work. She called the record more personal than any of her earlier ones. I Blame You uses a sample of the Mary Jane Girls, and Like This samples Black Heat and Doug E. Fresh. The reviews were mostly positive. Like This earned a Grammy nomination for Best R&B Performance.
werk/ledisi-the-truth.listen: Listen to I Blame You and notice the sample beneath the song and what Ledisi sings: can you hear how personal the lyrics sound?

werk/ledisi-turn-me-loose.text:
For her fifth album, Ledisi suffered from writer's block. She found the way out by listening to Them Changes by Buddy Miles from 1970. The album was released on 18 August 2009 by Verve Records. Unlike her earlier work, which leaned towards jazz and soul, it sounds decidedly funky. For the production she brought in Raphael Saadiq, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, and James Big Jim Wright, and she again worked with Rex Rideout, who had also steered the previous album, Lost & Found.

The title says what it is about: she did not want to be put in a box. Rock, blues, classic soul, funk and hip hop run into one another. As a tribute to Buddy Miles, she also recorded Them Changes herself, as a bonus track. The reviews were generally favourable, and the album received two Grammy nominations, including for Best R&B Album.
werk/ledisi-turn-me-loose.listen: Listen to Turn Me Loose and notice the funk groove. One reviewer heard in this track the punchy grooves of the old Stax.

werk/lee-konitz-inside-hi-fi.text:
Inside Hi-Fi was released in 1956 by Atlantic and contains the first recording on which Lee Konitz plays tenor saxophone, alongside his usual alto saxophone. The eight tracks feature two accompanying groups. In the first four we hear the guitarist Billy Bauer and the bassist Arnold Fishkin, in the last four the pianist Sal Mosca and the bassist Peter Ind. The drummer Dick Scott is heard on all tracks, under his pseudonym Tox Drohar.

Konitz himself wrote Kary's Trance and Cork 'n' Bib, and Peter Ind contributed Nesuhi's Instant. The rest consists of standards such as Everything Happens to Me, All of Me, Star Eyes and Indiana. Scott Yanow of AllMusic finds all eight performances well played and swinging.
werk/lee-konitz-inside-hi-fi.listen: Listen in Kary's Trance to how the saxophone sounds in a small group with guitar, bass and drums, without piano.

werk/lee-konitz-lee-konitz-with-warne-ma.text:
This studio album from 1955 brings together two saxophonists: Lee Konitz on alto and Warne Marsh on tenor. It was recorded on 14 June 1955 at Coastal Studios in New York, for Atlantic. The pianist Sal Mosca plays on most of the tracks, Ronnie Ball on one. The guitarist Billy Bauer, the bassist Oscar Pettiford and the drummer Kenny Clarke are also heard. Nesuhi Ertegun was the producer.

Billboard found the album remarkable for its excellent modern playing and its successful use of old and new jazz sources. The Guardian wrote that the two saxophonists play without much emphasis and almost coolly, but that their melodic ingenuity is astonishing. BBC Music praised the graceful, intelligent and swinging playing. The Penguin Guide to Jazz counts the record among its core collection.
werk/lee-konitz-lee-konitz-with-warne-ma.listen: Listen to Donna Lee and notice how alto and tenor play together and who takes the lead at which moment.

werk/lee-morgan-candy.text:
Candy is a studio album by the trumpeter Lee Morgan, recorded on 18 November 1957 and 2 February 1958 and released in late 1958 by Blue Note. Morgan plays here in a quartet with the pianist Sonny Clark, the bassist Doug Watkins and the drummer Art Taylor. Alfred Lion produced, Rudy Van Gelder recorded it and Reid Miles designed the cover.

AllMusic praises Morgan's tone: sweet, with fluid playing and a clear, joyful expression. He would later become an excellent songwriter, but on this album tracks such as Since I Fell for You by Buddy Johnson and C.T.A. by Jimmy Heath give him all the room to show what he can do.
werk/lee-morgan-candy.listen: Listen in Since I Fell for You to the tone of the trumpet and notice how fluidly Morgan plays the melody.

werk/lee-morgan-city-lights.text:
Lee Morgan recorded City Lights on 25 August 1957, when he was only nineteen. Blue Note released the record the following year. It is a sextet: besides the trumpeter, the trombonist Curtis Fuller, George Coleman on tenor and alto saxophone, the pianist Ray Bryant, the bassist Paul Chambers and the drummer Art Taylor play. Alfred Lion produced and Rudy Van Gelder handled the recording.

AllMusic found Morgan in excellent form and saw how he held his own alongside his impressive accompanists. The reviewer names City Lights, You're Mine You and Just By Myself as highlights. DownBeat gave the album four out of five stars in October 1958 and praised Morgan's control of his instrument and his creativity.
werk/lee-morgan-city-lights.listen: Listen in City Lights to Morgan's trumpet and notice how he makes himself heard between trombone and saxophone.

werk/lee-morgan-dizzy-atmosphere.text:
Dizzy Atmosphere is an album featuring members of Dizzy Gillespie's orchestra: the trombonist Al Grey, the saxophonist Billy Mitchell and the trumpeter Lee Morgan. It was recorded in 1957 and released on the Specialty label. The baritone saxophonist Billy Root, the pianist Wynton Kelly, the bassist Paul West and the drummer Charlie Persip also take part. Most of the pieces were arranged by Roger Spotts, three by Benny Golson.

Scott Yanow of AllMusic called the music modern bop for its time. He pointed to the Dishwater, which lasts more than ten minutes, to Over the Rainbow and to an early performance of Golson's Whisper Not. Morgan plays remarkably well throughout the record, Yanow wrote, and he was only eighteen years old at the time. The CD also includes alternate takes of three tracks.
werk/lee-morgan-dizzy-atmosphere.listen: Listen to Dishwater, the longest piece on the record, and notice how the soloists use the space of more than twelve minutes.

werk/lee-morgan-indeed.text:
Indeed! is the debut album of the trumpeter Lee Morgan. He recorded it on 4 November 1956 and it was released that same year by Blue Note. Alfred Lion produced, and Rudy Van Gelder was at the controls.

He plays in a quintet with the alto saxophonist Clarence Sharpe and a rhythm section of the pianist Horace Silver, the bassist Wilbur Ware and the drummer Philly Joe Jones. The repertoire is diverse and comes from various writers: Roccus by Silver, Reggie of Chester and Stand By by Benny Golson, and Little T by Donald Byrd. The pieces last from almost four to well over eight minutes. AllMusic gave the record three stars. The CD also contains an alternate take of Little T.
werk/lee-morgan-indeed.listen: Listen to Roccus and notice the pianist Horace Silver, who wrote this piece and also plays on it himself.

werk/lee-morgan-the-sidewinder.text:
Lee Morgan recorded this album in 1964 at the Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, for the Blue Note label. He played trumpet in a quintet that included Joe Henderson on tenor saxophone and Billy Higgins on drums. He wrote all the tracks himself.

The title track, probably his best-known composition, is a soulful boogaloo with a swaying twenty-four-bar theme. It became a jazz standard and also charted as a single in the United States. Blue Note initially pressed only 4,000 copies, but these sold out within days. The album became the label's best-selling record and saved the label from near bankruptcy. The track was also used in a TV commercial. Blue Note then wanted more records like it, and Morgan's next albums followed the same template. In 2024 the Library of Congress added the album to the National Recording Registry.
werk/lee-morgan-the-sidewinder.listen: Listen in The Sidewinder to the swaying theme and notice the rhythm section of bass and drums underneath.

werk/lee-scratch-perry-battle-of-armagid.text:
Battle of Armagideon (Millionaire Liquidator) was released in 1986 on Trojan Records. Lee Scratch Perry made it with his backing group of the moment, the Upsetters. He produced it himself, together with Mark Downie, who also designed the cover. Perry sings and plays percussion and harmonica. We also hear guitars, keyboards, bass, drums, saxophone and trombone.

The record was reissued on CD in 1988 and again in 2001. Trouser Press heard a kind of return to his best form: a dense production that nevertheless sounds contemporary, with cryptic lyrics in a stream of consciousness. The Spin Alternative Record Guide called it his best album of the 1980s.
werk/lee-scratch-perry-battle-of-armagid.listen: Listen to I Am a Madman and notice the dense production and the strange, flowing lyrics.

werk/lenny-kuhr-de-troubadour.text: On 29 March 1969, the nineteen-year-old Lenny Kuhr won the Eurovision Song Contest in Madrid with De troubadour, jointly with three other countries, which all had the same number of points. She had co-written the song herself and sang it with her guitar, as a modern singer-songwriter. De troubadour is about a medieval singer who travels from town to town. It was the third Dutch victory.
werk/lenny-kuhr-de-troubadour.listen: Hear how the song begins with only guitar and voice, and then grows bigger with an orchestra.

werk/les-mccann-comment.text:
This album from 1969 was released by Atlantic. The pianist and singer Les McCann chose a very different tone here from that of Swiss Movement and Second Movement, the electric collaborations with Eddie Harris that came before and after. Comment is a quiet, gentle collection, mostly of love songs.

A large group of studio musicians plays on the album, including Ron Carter on bass and Billy Cobham on drums. Roberta Flack sings on the first two tracks. William Fischer wrote the arrangements for some of the tracks, with trumpets and trombones among other instruments. The closing song Yours Is My Heart Alone is by Franz Lehár and is given a choir here. The title track is by Yusuf Rahman and Charles Wright. AllMusic gives the album three stars and calls it a mellow set.
werk/les-mccann-comment.listen: Listen to How Many Broken Wings and notice the calm love-song tone of the vocals, with Roberta Flack nearby.

werk/les-mccann-jazz-waltz.text:
The pianist Les McCann recorded this record in 1963 with The Jazz Crusaders and released it on the Pacific Jazz label. Besides McCann, who plays piano, organ and electric piano, we hear the members of the Crusaders: Wayne Henderson on trombone, Wilton Felder on tenor saxophone, Joe Sample on piano and organ, Bobby Haynes on bass and Stix Hooper on drums. The repertoire is mixed. It includes pieces by Fats Waller, Bobby Timmons, Toots Thielemans and Miles Davis, and also compositions by McCann himself, such as Damascus.

AllMusic gave the album three stars.
werk/les-mccann-jazz-waltz.listen: Listen to All Blues, a composition by Miles Davis, and notice how the horns of The Jazz Crusaders and McCann's piano alternate.

werk/les-mccann-les-mccann-sings.text:
Les McCann is best known as a pianist, but on this 1961 album for the Pacific Jazz label he is also the centre of attention as a singer. He plays piano and sings twelve songs, from Sweet Georgia Brown and Bye Bye Blackbird to On the Street Where You Live. The bassist Herbie Lewis and the drummer Ron Jefferson form the rhythm section. On some of the tracks a large ensemble joins in, with trumpets, trombones, saxophones and sometimes strings, arranged and conducted by Gerald Wilson. On Next Spring we hear, among others, the saxophonist Ben Webster and the organist Richard Groove Holmes.

The AllMusic reviewer called the record a super-good set of soul jazz and blues at their best.
werk/les-mccann-les-mccann-sings.listen: Listen to Next Spring and notice the tenor saxophone of Ben Webster, who plays only on this track, together with organ and guitar.

werk/les-paul-how-high-the-moon.text: On 4 January 1951, the guitarist Les Paul and the singer Mary Ford recorded How High the Moon in their apartment in Queens. Les Paul built up layer upon layer with a tape recorder: he played all the guitars himself and Ford sang her part several times. This is called overdubbing. The record spent nine weeks at number one. From then on you could build a record in the studio, instead of just capturing a performance.
werk/les-paul-how-high-the-moon.listen: Hear how many more guitars and voices sound than two people could play at once. Everything is layered.

werk/linda-ronstadt-don-t-cry-now.text:
Linda Ronstadt recorded for Capitol early in her career, but got out of that contract earlier than planned in order to sign with David Geffen's Asylum Records. Don't Cry Now was her first album there and the first with the producer Peter Asher, with whom she would later make thirteen albums. Recording began in 1972 and lasted a year, partly because she went on tour with Neil Young. First John Boylan and JD Souther produced, after which Asher finished the album.

Many tracks are covers, including Silver Threads and Golden Needles, Sail Away by Randy Newman, Desperado by the Eagles and I Believe in You by Neil Young. Souther wrote three tracks, including the title song. Reviewers praised her singing. Allmusic called it her first real hit record.
werk/linda-ronstadt-don-t-cry-now.listen: Listen to Desperado, a song by the Eagles, and notice how her voice carries the song.

werk/linda-ronstadt-hand-sown-home-grown.text:
Linda Ronstadt had had success with the folk trio the Stone Poneys, who scored a top twenty single in 1967 with Different Drum. When the other two members left, she chose a solo career, and Capitol Records wanted to invest in it. Because the band's songs had always come from Bob Kimmel, she went back to the country music of her youth. The producer Chip Douglas, who had previously worked with The Monkees and The Turtles, helped her blend country and rock. She looked for musicians who could play Nashville songs with a Californian twist.

The album was released in March 1969 and was her first to carry her name alone. It includes covers of Bob Dylan, Randy Newman and John D. Loudermilk, and of Only Daddy That'll Walk the Line, which was rewritten for her as Only Mama That'll Walk the Line. Rolling Stone called it a distinctive approach to country as rock.
werk/linda-ronstadt-hand-sown-home-grown.listen: Listen to The Only Mama That'll Walk the Line and notice the singer delivering a familiar country song from a female perspective. Can you hear how country and rock blend here?

werk/linda-ronstadt-silk-purse.text:
Silk Purse was released on 13 April 1970 by Capitol Records and was Linda Ronstadt's second solo album. As on her first solo record, it centred on country, the music she had heard as a child. The album was recorded in January and February 1970 at two studios in Nashville, partly also in San Francisco. The producer Elliot Mazer worked with the Nashville session musicians of Area Code 615, who play on the record.

It contains new songs, such as Long Long Time by Gary White and Louise by Paul Siebel, about a prostitute. There are also covers of Hank Williams and Mel Tillis, a gospel song and an R&B song. Long Long Time became her first entry on the American and Canadian charts. Critics praised her voice. Robert Christgau called Lovesick Blues and Long Long Time brilliant. It was her first album on the American chart.
werk/linda-ronstadt-silk-purse.listen: Listen to Long Long Time and notice the emotion in the voice. Listen above all to the voice, because that is what critics wrote about most.

werk/link-wray-be-what-you-want-to.text:
Be What You Want To is a 1973 album by the American guitarist Link Wray. It was recorded in 1972 with many guest musicians: Jerry Garcia plays guitar and pedal steel, Commander Cody piano and keyboards, David Bromberg acoustic and electric guitar. Thomas Jefferson Kaye produced the record. Tom Salisbury plays organ, piano and clavinet and wrote the arrangements for horns and strings.

The eleven tracks are largely the guitarist's own work. There are also Lawdy Miss Clawdy by Lloyd Price and All Cried Out, written by Mann Curtis and Michel Deborah. The title track lasts almost six minutes and opens the record. Besides the guitars, violin, cello, trumpet and saxophones, among others, take part, so that the band is large and varied.
werk/link-wray-be-what-you-want-to.listen: Listen to Lawdy Miss Clawdy, which lasts only a little over two minutes, and notice what guitar and band do with this song by Lloyd Price.

werk/linkin-park-hybrid-theory.text:
Hybrid Theory is Linkin Park's debut album, released on 24 October 2000. The band grew out of the rap group Xero, which Mike Shinoda and two school friends started in 1996. The singer Chester Bennington joined the group in 1999, and the producer Don Gilmore recorded the record in four months in North Hollywood. The title refers to the earlier band name and to the combining of styles. The lyrics deal largely with Bennington's youth, with drugs, alcohol and his parents' divorce.

The sound is usually called nu metal, rap metal or rap rock. Shinoda raps in the verses, Bennington sings and screams. One Step Closer is known for the shout "Shut up when I'm talkin' to you!". In the End revolves around a piano riff by Shinoda. Four tracks were released as singles and made the band world famous. The record was a great commercial success and is called the best-selling debut record since Appetite for Destruction. Crawling won a Grammy.
werk/linkin-park-hybrid-theory.listen: Listen to In the End and notice the piano riff with which it begins, and how Shinoda raps in the verses and Bennington sings the choruses.

werk/linkin-park-living-things.text:
Living Things is the band's fifth album and was released in June 2012. Recording began in March 2011 and lasted until April 2012, at NRG Recording Studios. Mike Shinoda and Rick Rubin produced, as before on Minutes to Midnight and A Thousand Suns. It was the last album that Rubin made with the band. After years of experimenting, the band members said they finally felt at home on familiar ground.

The title refers to the many personal subjects on the record. The sound combines elements of the four earlier albums: the energy of the older work with the innovation of the newer. Burn It Down was the first single, followed by Lost in the Echo, Powerless and Castle of Glass. Lies Greed Misery premiered in May 2012 after a worldwide search on the internet. In the United States the album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200.
werk/linkin-park-living-things.listen: Listen to Burn It Down, the first single, and notice how the band brings old and new sound together.

werk/linkin-park-meteora.text:
After the debut Hybrid Theory and the remix album Reanimation, Linkin Park wanted to make a second studio album that would extend the sound with more experimental ideas. The band wrote around 80 demos while on tour, worked on the pre-production in Mike Shinoda's home studio and recorded the album with the producer Don Gilmore. It was the first album with the bassist Dave Farrell. The recording took almost a year, and during mastering there was even security to prevent leaks.

The sound closely resembles that of the debut: heavy guitars, rap, scratches and vocals about anger, doubt and recovery. The intro of Somewhere I Belong came about when Shinoda and Joe Hahn reversed and processed a guitar recording. In Breaking the Habit we hear strings, arranged by David Campbell. Critics were mostly positive, although some felt the record resembled its predecessor too much.
werk/linkin-park-meteora.listen: Listen to the beginning of Somewhere I Belong: the floating, sweeping sound of the intro is a reversed guitar part.

werk/linkin-park-minutes-to-midnight.text:
After Meteora, Linkin Park set to work on a third album in 2003, but solo projects by Mike Shinoda and Chester Bennington temporarily halted the work. The band then returned with the producer Rick Rubin, and that led to a different direction. The recording took fourteen months, much longer than on the previous records, and the group wrote more than a hundred songs. The title refers to the Doomsday Clock.

The band largely left the nu metal sound behind and opted for a more restrained, more classic rock sound with influences from punk and hip hop. There is much less rapping and Joe Hahn's scratches have moved into the background. For the first time guitar solos are heard, and six tracks received strings by David Campbell. The album received mixed reviews, but Rolling Stone placed it at number twenty-five among the records of 2007.
werk/linkin-park-minutes-to-midnight.listen: Listen in Hands Held High to the combination of church organ and military march rhythm, over which Mike Shinoda raps almost the entire song.

werk/linkin-park-numb.text: In September 2003 Numb by Linkin Park was released as a single, from the album Meteora. The band blended metal with hip hop and electronics: nu metal. The singer Chester Bennington sang and screamed, and Mike Shinoda rapped and made beats. Numb is about someone who feels never good enough for others. It became one of the most streamed rock songs ever, long after Bennington died in 2017.
werk/linkin-park-numb.listen: Hear the piano melody and the electronic beat beneath the guitars. Bennington sings the chorus almost screaming.

werk/lionel-richie-can-t-slow-down.text:
Can't Slow Down was Lionel Richie's second solo album, after his time with the Commodores. It was released on 14 October 1983 by Motown. According to Christgau, the bouncy, internationally flavoured dance music suited Richie better than the funk of his old group, and his ballads were an improvement too. On All Night Long (All Night) a large choir sings along in a song that Q later described as a hymn to the good life.

The album reached the top spot on the American album chart and spent 59 consecutive weeks in the top ten. All five singles reached the top ten of the Hot 100, with All Night Long (All Night) and Hello at number one. In 1985 it won the Grammy for Album of the Year, ahead of Born in the U.S.A. and Purple Rain. It became his best-selling record, with more than twenty million copies worldwide.
werk/lionel-richie-can-t-slow-down.listen: Listen to All Night Long (All Night) and notice the choir singing along. Hear how festive the vocals and rhythms together make a song full of good vibes.

werk/lionel-richie-dancing-on-the-ceilin.text:
Lionel Richie began this album in 1985, while he was also busy with We Are the World. His first two solo albums had been great successes. The new album was at first to be called Say You, Say Me and to appear in December 1985. But he no longer felt like those songs because of what he saw around him, and rewrote them. The recording ultimately took well over a year and a half. The record took its title from the next single, Dancing on the Ceiling, and was released in August 1986.

Richie wanted to present a mixture of sounds. Reviewers responded mostly positively. Rolling Stone singled out Say You, Say Me for praise, while Ballerina Girl was criticised for its sentimentality. The album topped the American Billboard 200 and the title song reached number two in the United States. After that, Richie took a long break of ten years.
werk/lionel-richie-dancing-on-the-ceilin.listen: Listen to Dancing On the Ceiling and notice what sounds you hear. Does it fit the idea of a mixture of styles?

werk/lisa-gerrard-duality.text:
Duality is a collaboration between Lisa Gerrard and Pieter Bourke and was released in 1998. It was her second album since the end of Dead Can Dance: the band officially ceased to exist that year. The album was nominated for an ARIA Award for Best World Music Album.

The record has a striking afterlife in film music. The beginning of Shadow Magnet partly influenced the music at the start of the Gladiator soundtrack. Nadir (Synchronicity) was originally intended for the closing of that film, but because of rights issues a piece inspired by it was used instead. Tempest and Sacrifice were heard in the film The Insider.
werk/lisa-gerrard-duality.listen: Listen to Shadow Magnet and notice the opening: it influenced the music at the beginning of the Gladiator soundtrack.

werk/lisa-gerrard-the-mirror-pool.text:
The Mirror Pool is Lisa Gerrard's first solo album and was released in 1995 by 4AD, a year before Spiritchaser, the last album that Dead Can Dance released before the band split up. The music dates from the years 1988 to 1995 and contains work that did not fit on her band's albums. It is largely orchestral and written for voice.

The singer described the title as a reference to African music, in which musicians were said to come into contact with spirits, and to a mirror in which the listener finds themselves reflected. She produced the record herself. The Victorian Philharmonic Orchestra plays on it. Persian Love Song is a traditional song from Shiraz, and Largo is the famous aria from Handel's opera Serse. La Bas, Celon and Gloradin were heard in the film Heat.
werk/lisa-gerrard-the-mirror-pool.listen: Listen to Largo and notice how a famous aria from an opera by Handel stands here among other work on this record.

werk/little-eva-the-loco-motion.text: Eva Boyd was the babysitter of Carole King and Gerry Goffin. Because she could sing well, she recorded the demo of The Loco-Motion, the trial recording with which writers tried to sell a song to an artist. That demo sounded so good that it was released as a single, under the name Little Eva. On 25 August 1962 the song was at the top of the American chart. Writing and release lay very close together.
werk/little-eva-the-loco-motion.listen: Hear the handclaps and the girl explaining how to do the dance. A demo that became a worldwide hit.

werk/little-richard-here-s-little-richar.text:
This debut album by Little Richard was released on 4 March 1957 as Specialty's first twelve-inch LP. Art Rupe put it together from six hits of 1955 and 1956 and six new tracks. The producer was Bumps Blackwell, and almost everything was recorded in New Orleans, with True, Fine Mama and She's Got It in Los Angeles as the exceptions. Tutti Frutti began as a rough song that the songwriter Dorothy LaBostrie cleaned up. It is celebrated for its screamed opening phrase and the piano playing in straight eighths, which gave R&B a new pulse.

Long Tall Sally is also fast, with falsetto and hammering boogie piano. The album reached number thirteen on the Billboard chart, his highest placing. Critics regard it as one of the records from which rock 'n' roll grew, and it ranked high in lists by Rolling Stone and Time. Singers such as Otis Redding and James Brown borrowed from it, as did the Beatles and the Rolling Stones later.
werk/little-richard-here-s-little-richar.listen: Listen in Tutti Frutti to the screamed chorus and to the pianist playing in straight eighths, a pattern that would later drive much R&B and rock.

werk/little-richard-the-fabulous-little-.text:
The Fabulous Little Richard is Little Richard's third studio album and the last from his rock and roll period. It was released seventeen months after he left Specialty Records. Richard had returned to his faith and turned away from the music that had made him famous. He would later reverse that decision briefly, but this album ended his peak period.

The record was assembled from outtakes and other leftover recordings, on which Richard sounds somewhat softer than before. On just over half of the tracks a female chorus, the Stewart Sisters, was added to make the music more accessible. The sleeve notes said this came closer to the church singing he had grown up with. Kansas City also contains lyric lines from his own Hey, Hey, Hey, Hey, something The Beatles later had to credit when they covered the song.
werk/little-richard-the-fabulous-little-.listen: Listen to Kansas City and notice the saxophones and Richard's raw voice above the rhythm of piano and drums.

werk/little-richard-the-rill-thing.text:
The Rill Thing was released in August 1970 and was Little Richard's first album for Reprise Records. It was regarded as a comeback after three years without new records and after his acclaimed performance at the Atlantic City Pop Festival. He produced the record himself for the first time and put his own money into it. The arrangements lean on the soul and R&B of the time, with an emphasis on bass and guitar.

Freedom Blues reached the Billboard top 50, his biggest American hit in thirteen years. The album itself did not chart. The closing consists of two covers: Lovesick Blues and I Saw Her Standing There by the Beatles. The title track lasts well over ten minutes and is an instrumental jam. Rolling Stone called the record an artistic success on its release.
werk/little-richard-the-rill-thing.listen: Listen in Dew Drop Inn to the intro, which borrows the drum part of Keep A-Knockin', and to the screaming vocals and the rolling piano.

werk/living-colour-vivid.text:
Vivid is Living Colour's debut album and was released on 2 May 1988 by Epic Records. It became one of the most popular albums of that year. It reached number six on the American Billboard 200 and went double platinum. Ed Stasium produced most of it. Mick Jagger produced two tracks, played harmonica on Broken Hearts and sang on Glamour Boys.

The sound is hard to put under one heading. There is hard rock, heavy metal and funk, with influences from soul, jazz, rap and punk. On Funny Vibe, Chuck D of Public Enemy raps along, with a contribution from Flavor Flav. Critics praised the blend of influences and the social criticism in tracks such as Funny Vibe and Open Letter (To a Landord). One reviewer later called the record an important document of Black rock music. It was included in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.
werk/living-colour-vivid.listen: Listen to Funny Vibe and notice how the rap of Chuck D and the commentary of Flavor Flav fit into a rock song.

werk/lou-donaldson-light-foot.text:
Light Foot is an album by the alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson, recorded on 14 December 1958 at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, and released by Blue Note. He plays with his quintet: the pianist Herman Foster, the bassist Peck Morrison, the drummer Jimmy Wormworth and Ray Barretto on congas. Alfred Lion was the producer.

The saxophonist is still firmly rooted in bop here, but the tempos are lower and the influence of the blues comes through more strongly. The pieces are hard bop, not straightforward bop as on earlier records. The repertoire consists of original work, such as the title song and Hog Maw, and of well-known songs such as Green Eyes and Stella By Starlight. The critics were divided. DownBeat felt the material did not fully show his abilities. AllMusic gave three stars and called the material and the playing at times uneven.
werk/lou-donaldson-light-foot.listen: Listen to Stella By Starlight and notice how the alto saxophone plays the familiar melody and what the rhythm section, with congas, does underneath.

werk/lou-donaldson-lou-takes-off.text:
Lou Takes Off is an album by the alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson, recorded on 15 December 1957 and released a year later by Blue Note. It is a sextet session: alongside him play the trumpeter Donald Byrd and the trombonist Curtis Fuller, with the pianist Sonny Clark, the bassist Jamil Nasser and the drummer Art Taylor as the rhythm section. Alfred Lion produced, Rudy Van Gelder recorded.

According to the saxophonist himself, Blue Note initially thought little of the record, nor of the new musicians. The AllMusic review sees the album as a moment of stylistic change, after which his music moved away from bop and more towards rhythm and blues. The record does not break new ground, the reviewer says, but it is a solid, swinging session with high-level playing. The album includes Sputnik, Dewey Square and Groovin' High, among others.
werk/lou-donaldson-lou-takes-off.listen: Listen to Dewey Square and notice how the saxophone, the trumpet and the trombone alternate, before the rhythm section gets the space again.

werk/lou-donaldson-quartet-quintet-sexte.text:
Quartet/Quintet/Sextet was released in 1957 on Blue Note, but the recordings are older: they date from 20 June and 19 November 1952 and 22 August 1954. The quartet consists of Lou Donaldson with Horace Silver, Gene Ramey and Art Taylor. In the quintet the trumpeter Blue Mitchell is added. The sextet has a new line-up with Kenny Dorham, Matthew Gee, Elmo Hope, Percy Heath and Art Blakey.

The sessions had previously appeared on New Faces, New Sounds and on Lou Donaldson Sextet, Volume 2. The producer was Alfred Lion and Rudy Van Gelder recorded the 1954 session. AllMusic heard in Donaldson a player whose tone was not yet as full as it later became, but with fluent technique and fine phrasing, within bop and hard bop.
werk/lou-donaldson-quartet-quintet-sexte.listen: Listen in Down Here On The Ground to Donaldson's alto saxophone and notice his fast playing and his phrasing.

werk/lou-reed-berlin.text:
The producer Bob Ezrin noticed that the stories in Lou Reed's songs had strong beginnings but never an ending. He wanted to know what had happened to the couple in the song Berlin on Reed's first solo record. This is how Reed's third solo album came about, released in October 1973 by RCA: a concept album about Jim and Caroline, a doomed couple, with themes such as drugs, prostitution, depression, domestic violence and suicide. In The Kids you hear children crying for their mother.

Some of the songs Reed had written earlier, sometimes for the Velvet Underground. The title track was rewritten here for piano alone. The music has been described as art rock and orchestral rock. Rolling Stone called the album a disaster in 1973, it reached number seven in England, and appreciation grew later. In 2007 Reed performed the album on stage, with a band of thirty and twelve choir singers, and that concert was filmed.
werk/lou-reed-berlin.listen: Listen in The Kids to the crying children that can be heard in the song, and to how that makes Caroline's story oppressive.

werk/lou-reed-coney-island-baby.text:
Coney Island Baby is Lou Reed's sixth solo album and was released in December 1975 by RCA. Anthony DeCurtis called it perhaps the most romantic album of his career. Many songs were inspired by his girlfriend at the time, Rachel Humphreys. In the title song he mentions her by name, alongside the elementary school P.S. 192 in Brooklyn that he attended himself. The Velvet Underground had already recorded She's My Best Friend in 1969, but it only appeared in 1985.

Reed and Godfrey Diamond produced the album with a clear production and a band that, according to Rolling Stone, was the best since the Velvet Underground, with strong drumming by Michael Suchorsky. He dropped the vocal style of the preceding years for more assured, more expressive singing. The Rough Guide calls it his most pleasant soft rock album, with his best humour on A Gift.
werk/lou-reed-coney-island-baby.listen: Listen to the title track Coney Island Baby and notice the line in which a greeting goes out to Rachel and the children of P.S. 192.

werk/lou-reed-metal-machine-music.text:
In July 1975 RCA released Metal Machine Music as a double album, Lou Reed's fifth studio album, only to withdraw it from sale again three weeks later. The record contains no songs or recognisable compositions, only layers of feedback and distortion at varying speeds. Reed tuned all the guitar strings to the same note and was influenced by the drone sounds of La Monte Young. He also said he had listened a lot to Xenakis and tried to release the album on the classical label RCA Red Seal.

It became the most returned album in RCA's history, although about a hundred thousand are said to have been sold. Critics rejected it. Lester Bangs saw integrity in it and the biographer Victor Bockris later called it a forerunner of New York punk. It also opened the door to Reed's later experimental work.
werk/lou-reed-metal-machine-music.listen: Listen to Metal Machine Music, Pt. 1 and notice how feedback and distortion take the place of melody and rhythm.

werk/lou-reed-sally-can-t-dance.text:
Sally Can't Dance is Lou Reed's fourth solo album and was released in September 1974 by RCA Records. Steve Katz and Reed produced. It is the first solo record without songs that he had previously recorded with the Velvet Underground, and the first to be recorded in the United States. It remained his highest-charting album in America, reaching number 10.

N.Y. Stars is about imitators who copied his style. Kill Your Sons refers to his time in a psychiatric clinic as a teenager. On Billy, about a schoolmate with more normal ambitions, his old Velvet Underground bandmate Doug Yule plays bass. After Transformer, Berlin and Rock 'n' Roll Animal, the reviews were mostly negative, and Reed himself was dissatisfied with the production.
werk/lou-reed-sally-can-t-dance.listen: Listen in Billy to the bass guitar of Doug Yule, Reed's old bandmate in the Velvet Underground.

werk/lou-reed-transformer.text:
Lou Reed had had little success with his first solo album. David Bowie, an early fan of the Velvet Underground, used his fame to support him and produced the follow-up together with Mick Ronson at Trident Studios in London. Four of the eleven tracks Reed had written back in the days of the Velvet Underground, such as Satellite of Love and Andy's Chest; the tempo went down. Ronson played guitar, piano and recorder and wrote the strings for Perfect Day.

Walk on the Wild Side, about sexual orientation, gender identity, prostitution and drugs, became his biggest single, although it was edited or banned in some countries. The song is based on people from Andy Warhol's Factory. Vicious grew out of a remark by Warhol. The album turned a cult figure into an international star and is regarded as an influential landmark of glam rock.
werk/lou-reed-transformer.listen: Listen in Perfect Day to Mick Ronson's strings and to how the vocals deliberately stay beneath them.

werk/louis-armstrong-louis-and-the-angel.text:
Louis and the Angels is a studio album that was recorded on 29 and 30 January 1957 and released later that year by Decca. It is loosely a concept album: all the songs refer to angels. Sy Oliver wrote all the arrangements and conducted a choir and orchestra. Besides Armstrong we hear, among others, Lucky Thompson and Phil Urso on tenor saxophone and Billy Kyle on piano.

AllMusic calls the record obscure, but with a strange appeal. Armstrong plays a few good trumpet solos and sounds cheerful throughout the record. The album is more commercial than his usual recordings of the period, but according to the reviewer it sticks in the mind better than you would expect.
werk/louis-armstrong-louis-and-the-angel.listen: Listen in The Prisoner's Song to the joke the singer makes when the word angel finally turns up in the lyrics.

werk/louis-armstrong-louis-armstrong-pla.text:
This studio album from 1954 was made by Louis Armstrong and His All Stars and consists of songs by the blues composer W.C. Handy. George Avakian produced. In the band play Trummy Young on trombone, Barney Bigard on clarinet, Billy Kyle on piano, Arvell Shaw on bass and Barrett Deems on drums. The singer Velma Middleton sings on a number of tracks.

AllMusic calls the record the trumpeter's best of the 1950s and essential music for any serious jazz collection. The 1986 CD edition altered the album considerably, with different versions of many tracks. Only the 1997 reissue restored the original. It added a short interview of Handy himself by Avakian and rehearsal versions.
werk/louis-armstrong-louis-armstrong-pla.listen: Listen in St. Louis Blues, at almost nine minutes the longest track on the record, to how trumpet and vocals shape the familiar theme.

werk/ludovico-einaudi-i-giorni.text:
I Giorni was released in 2001. The title means The Days in English. The album contains fourteen pieces by the Italian pianist Ludovico Einaudi. Four of them are named Melodia Africana or Canzone Africana, numbered I to IV, and they recur between the other pieces.

The title track received the most attention much later. In June 2011 Greg James played it on BBC Radio 1, and on 12 June it reached number 32 on the UK Singles Chart. The piano version had already been used in a BBC advertisement for arts and culture programmes. Airtel, an Indian telecom company, also used the piece in November 2010 for the launch of its 3G services. In 2016 it was heard in an Amazon Prime commercial. In 2022 the single was certified gold in the United Kingdom.
werk/ludovico-einaudi-i-giorni.listen: Listen in I Giorni to the piano: notice how simple the melody is and how long it lingers.

werk/ludovico-einaudi-le-onde.text:
Le onde is a 1996 album by the Italian pianist Ludovico Einaudi. It is based on the novel The Waves by the British writer Virginia Woolf and was his first solo album for piano. In the CD booklet he sketches an image of a long, endless beach where a man walks and perhaps meets no one. Only the waves change, always the same and yet different.

That image resonates in the title piece, Le onde. It is slow and flowing. The music is divided into sections that are repeated until a coda closes the piece. The right hand plays the melody, the left hand plays long, fast arpeggios with a recognisable chord pattern that keeps returning. In the chorus the key changes and new motifs are added. The album was very successful with a broad audience, especially in Italy and the United Kingdom.
werk/ludovico-einaudi-le-onde.listen: Listen to Le Onde and notice the left hand, which runs beneath the melody in flowing arpeggios.

werk/luis-fonsi-abrazar-la-vida.text:
Abrazar la vida was released on 28 October 2003 and is the fifth album by the singer Luis Fonsi. The record opens with ¿Quién Te Dijo Eso?, a plaintive love song in the torch song tradition. The title track follows, with a more R&B-like colour but still full of wistfulness. The album also contains more exuberant work: Yo Te Propongo is an almost dizzying dance number in which Latin horns wind their way through the music. On La Fuerza de Mi Corazón, Christina Valemi sings along.

AllMusic gave the album three and a half stars. According to that review, the singer feels most at home as a modern crooner, and with this fifth album he casts a satisfying pop shadow.
werk/luis-fonsi-abrazar-la-vida.listen: Listen to Yo Te Propongo and notice the Latin horns winding through the song, and the tempo, which is almost dizzying.

werk/luis-fonsi-fight-the-feeling.text:
Fight the Feeling was released in 2002 and is the fourth album by the Puerto Rican singer Luis Fonsi. It is so far his only album in English. It has eleven tracks and came about with a large group of producers, including Cutfather, Harvey Mason Jr. and Rudy Pérez, with contributions from Kara DioGuardi.

The record opens with the title track Fight the Feeling, followed by tracks such as Secret, Turn It Up and Save Me. One song from the album later got a second life: Keep My Cool was covered in 2004 by the Korean singer BoA as Spark on her album My Name.
werk/luis-fonsi-fight-the-feeling.listen: Listen to the title track Fight the Feeling and notice how the singer comes across in English.

werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-nuthin-fancy.text:
Nuthin' Fancy is Lynyrd Skynyrd's third album and was released in March 1975. It reached the top ten of the American album chart. It was the first record with the drummer Artimus Pyle. At the end of May that year the guitarist Ed King left the group in the middle of the Torture Tour. Al Kooper produced the album and played on it himself, on Moog, organ and piano.

The only single was Saturday Night Special, which reached number 27 on the Billboard chart. The critic Robert Christgau heard heavy rock in it with a funky undertone, and called the song a real killer. He also praised the singer Ronnie Van Zant, who had never used his hoarse baritone so subtly: with the smallest shifts he switches from boastful to warning.
werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-nuthin-fancy.listen: Listen to Saturday Night Special and notice how Ronnie Van Zant keeps changing the tone of the song with small shifts in his voice.

werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-pronounced-leh-nerd-.text:
Lynyrd Skynyrd's debut was released in August 1973 by MCA Records. The band already played most of the songs live. They had rehearsed endlessly in a remote rehearsal space near Jacksonville, Florida, which they called Hell House. The producer Al Kooper saw how well prepared they were: every note was fixed. The recording was at Studio One in Doraville, Georgia. During the sessions Ed King moved from bass to guitar when Leon Wilkeson returned. This is how the Three Guitar Army came about, with Allen Collins and Gary Rossington.

Kooper thought Simple Man too weak for the album. Ronnie Van Zant sent him to his car and had the band record the song without a producer. It became one of their best-known songs. Free Bird and Gimme Three Steps were also released as singles. The album was praised and put the band on the map of southern rock. Kooper also arranged a slot as the opening act for The Who.
werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-pronounced-leh-nerd-.listen: Listen in Free Bird to how the song changes in tempo and power.

werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-second-helping.text:
After the success of the debut record, Lynyrd Skynyrd's following grew rapidly in 1973, partly because the group opened for The Who on the Quadrophenia tour in the United States. The second album was released on 15 April 1974. For the first time Ed King, Allen Collins and Gary Rossington co-wrote with the singer Ronnie Van Zant.

The biggest hit is Sweet Home Alabama, an answer to Alabama and Southern Man by Neil Young. The song reached number 8 on the Hot 100 in August 1974. The three guitarists and the keyboardist stack simple riffs and feedback into a dense sound. On its release critics found the record not very innovative compared with the first, but later AllMusic called it tighter and more professional, and it earned a place on a list of the best boogie rock albums.
werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-second-helping.listen: Listen to Sweet Home Alabama and notice the three guitars building the riff, and the backing singers who sing along in the chorus.

werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-street-survivors.text:
Street Survivors was released on 17 October 1977. Three days later Lynyrd Skynyrd's chartered plane crashed. The singer Ronnie Van Zant, the guitarist Steve Gaines and the singer Cassie Gaines were killed, and the other band members were seriously injured. It was the last album with Van Zant and the only one with Steve Gaines. It was recorded twice: first in Miami with Tom Dowd, later in Doraville, Georgia. The second version was released.

Gaines was an important addition. He sings along on You Got That Right, wrote I Know a Little and sings his own blues Ain't No Good Life. What's Your Name became a hit, and That Smell warns against drugs. The original cover, with the band in front of burning buildings, was replaced after the disaster. The album received a great deal of attention and reached number five in the United States.
werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-street-survivors.listen: Listen to Ain't No Good Life. Notice that here it is not Van Zant but Steve Gaines who sings lead.

werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-sweet-home-alabama.text: In June 1974 Sweet Home Alabama by Lynyrd Skynyrd of Jacksonville was released, an answer to Southern Man and Alabama by Neil Young. The band took up the cause of the South, although the lyrics are ambiguous. Lynyrd Skynyrd was the best-known example of southern rock: blues, country and hard rock, with three guitarists. Young and the band, incidentally, respected one another. In 1977 three band members died in a plane crash.
werk/lynyrd-skynyrd-sweet-home-alabama.listen: The riff is D, C, G. The C is the flattened seventh of D, which is why it sounds Mixolydian, as is common in blues and country.

werk/madness-absolutely.text:
Absolutely is the second album by the English ska band Madness and was released on 26 September 1980 by Stiff Records. The producers were Clive Langer and Alan Winstanley. The title comes from an expression that the group's tour manager often used. The cover shows the band in front of Chalk Farm tube station in Camden.

The album sounds somewhat smoother than the rawer predecessor One Step Beyond..., with more R&B and funk. It yielded some of their biggest hits, such as Baggy Trousers and Embarrassment, and the instrumental The Return of the Los Palmas 7. The reviews were mixed to positive. One American reviewer thought the group an English version of the Blues Brothers, while AllMusic later wrote that the polish actually suits the three big singles.
werk/madness-absolutely.listen: Listen to The Return of the Los Palmas 7 and notice how the band, without a singer, still creates a recognisable, cheerful track.

werk/madness-keep-moving.text:
Keep Moving was released in February 1984 and was the last Madness album on Stiff. The band was already rehearsing for the record in February 1983, but the keyboardist Mike Barson, tired of the pressure of fame, spent that summer travelling around Europe in a camper van with his wife and dog. That held up the recording. In October he said he was quitting, and after a final performance at the end of 1983 he was gone. It was his last studio album with the group.

The title comes from the film The Bed Sitting Room, and the cover referred to the coming Olympic Games. Rolling Stone gave four out of five stars and praised the band's changing sound. Two singles reached the British top twenty. Wings of a Dove and The Sun and the Rain also belong to this period.
werk/madness-keep-moving.listen: Listen to Michael Caine and notice how Mike Barson, who had all but left the band, nevertheless still plays on it.

werk/madness-one-step-beyond.text:
One Step Beyond… was Madness's debut album and was released on 19 October 1979 by Stiff Records. Recording and mixing took about three weeks. It was the first record made by the production duo Clive Langer and Alan Winstanley, who would later produce more albums by the band. The title song is a piece by the Jamaican ska musician Prince Buster, with a spoken opening taken over from his song The Scorcher. The Prince is a tribute to Buster and a new recording of the group's first single. Madness, a song by Buster, is also on it.

The album reached number two on the British chart and stayed on it for more than a year. Critics called it a very enjoyable record, with its own blend of reggae and cheerful, fanfare-like madness. Together with the debut of the Specials, which came out on the same day, it made 2 Tone popular in England.
werk/madness-one-step-beyond.listen: Listen to One Step Beyond… and notice the spoken opening. Hear how the song then blends ska and cheerful madness.

werk/madness-the-rise-en-fall.text:
The Rise & Fall was released on 5 November 1982 by Stiff Records and is Madness's fourth studio album. The record began as a concept album about nostalgia for childhood, an idea of Chas Smash. The concept was dropped, but the theme remains audible, especially in Rise and Fall, Sunday Morning and Our House. The producers were Clive Langer and Alan Winstanley.

This is the band's most experimental record, with influences from jazz, English music hall and the East. Blue Skinned Beast is a sharp satire on the prime minister Margaret Thatcher and the Falklands War. A reviewer for AllMusic heard the influence of The Kinks and Ian Dury, but found the record unmistakably Madness, full of humour and cheerfulness. NME called it at the time the group's best record.
werk/madness-the-rise-en-fall.listen: Listen to Our House and notice how the song describes an ordinary family life, full of memories of home.

werk/madonna-bedtime-stories.text:
Bedtime Stories was released on 24 October 1994 as Madonna's sixth album. After all the fuss over Erotica, her book Sex and two films, she wanted to tone down the sexual theme and opted for R&B. She began with Shep Pettibone, but stopped when the demos came to resemble Erotica too much. She then worked with well-known producers: Dallas Austin, Babyface, Dave Hall and Nellee Hooper. It was the first time since her second album that she had worked this way.

Instead of lust, the songs are about romance, heartbreak, longing and regret. With Babyface she wrote Take a Bow and Forbidden Love, in his studio in Beverly Hills. Take a Bow spent seven weeks at the top of the American chart, her longest number 1. Critics appreciated the softer sound, others found it less striking than earlier work. Later the record is often seen as one of her best and most underrated. It received a Grammy nomination for Best Pop Album.
werk/madonna-bedtime-stories.listen: Listen to Take a Bow, a ballad by Madonna and Babyface, and notice how soft and direct the song sounds compared with the dance music of Erotica.
